lesson.title: Where It All Begins: Promoter Regions
lesson.summary: A promoter is a specific DNA sequence located just before a gene that RNA polymerase recognizes and binds to, marking exactly where transcription should start.
lesson.body:
As the previous chapter explained, RNA polymerase cannot simply start transcribing at a random point along a chromosome. Somewhere among millions or billions of base pairs of DNA, it needs to find the exact spot where a particular gene begins, and it needs to know which of the two DNA strands to use as the template. The promoter is the DNA sequence that solves this problem: a stretch of DNA positioned just upstream of (immediately before) a gene that RNA polymerase, often together with helper proteins, recognizes and binds to.

It is worth being clear about what a promoter is not: it is not itself transcribed into RNA as part of the gene's message. Its role is purely structural and recognition-based, acting as a landing pad and orientation marker for the transcription machinery rather than as coding sequence.

Many promoters contain short, recognizable sequence motifs that help position RNA polymerase correctly. A well known example found in many eukaryotic promoters is the TATA box, a short AT-rich sequence located a short distance upstream of the point where transcription actually begins. Sequences like this help the transcription machinery, including associated proteins that assist RNA polymerase in eukaryotic cells, assemble at precisely the right location and in the right orientation.

That orientation matters a great deal, because the two strands of the DNA double helix run antiparallel to each other. The way a promoter is arranged on the chromosome determines which of the two strands will serve as the template strand for that gene and, correspondingly, the direction in which RNA polymerase will travel as it transcribes.

Promoters are not all identical to one another, even within the same cell, and that variation is a major reason different genes are transcribed at different rates. A promoter sequence that is very effective at attracting RNA polymerase and its helper proteins will tend to produce a gene that is transcribed frequently and highly expressed, while a weaker promoter sequence will produce a gene that is transcribed only occasionally. This variability in promoter strength is one of the fundamental tools cells use to control gene expression, turning genes up or down as needed rather than transcribing every gene at the same constant rate.
